refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: systemd-keyring-setup.service is an early boot service that populates different keyrings with X.509 certificates found in the File Hierarchy for the Verification of OS Artifacts (VOA). After enrollment it seals the keyrings so that only certificates signed by an already enrolled key can be added anymore for the lifetime of the kernel. This allows the kernel to authenticate signatures with keys shipped by the OS vendor or configured by the administrator, without rebuilding the kernel or enrolling keys into the firmware.
The following keyrings are provisioned, each from a VOA context below the kernel-keyring role:

row.entry: Signatures on the root hash of dm-verity volumes, such as those of Discoverable Disk Images set up by systemd-veritysetup@.service8, systemd-dissect1 or the RootImage= setting of services
Built-in signatures of fs-verity protected files

refsect1.para: For each keyring the certificates below /etc/voa/, /run/voa/, /usr/local/share/voa/ and /usr/share/voa/ are looked up as OS/kernel-keyring/CONTEXT/x509/*-certificate.pem and OS/trust-anchor-kernel-keyring/CONTEXT/x509/*-certificate.pem. The part before -certificate.pem must consist of lowercase letters, digits, ., _ and -, like a credential name, other files are ignored. Both artifact verifiers and trust anchors end up in the same keyring. Every copy of a certificate in every load path counts. A certificate whose file name is masked via a symlink to /dev/null in any load path is ignored in all of them. A file holding more than one certificate is ignored. Symlinks are followed but the target must point inside the VOA hierarchy and carry the same file name. The OS identifiers looked up are derived from os-release5. The exact identifier composed of the ID=, VERSION_ID=, VARIANT_ID=, IMAGE_ID= and IMAGE_VERSION= fields as well as the bare ID=. Without ID= the identifier defaults to linux, which is combined with the other fields like an explicitly set ID=. If a field other than ID= contains characters the VOA specification does not allow, only the ID= is looked up. An ID= outside of the allowed set prevents the lookup. The keyring-setup.os credential below allows to specify identifiers explicitly. Both directories are searched.

The .dm-verity and .bpf keyrings are sealed empty by the kernel unless dm_verity.keyring_unsealed=1 and bpf.keyring_unsealed=1 are passed on the kernel command line. The kernel only uses them if they are sealed. The .fs-verity keyring is never sealed by the kernel and is used as soon as it holds a key. The service enrolls the keys and seals the keyrings. Note that it seals the keyrings even if no keys to enroll were found.

After keys have been enrolled the tool seals the keyring. After sealing, only certificates signed by a key already enrolled can be added. The permission to change the keyring's permissions or the restriction is removed. Thus, the set of trust anchors cannot be extended anymore once a keyring is fully setup.

The service runs in the initrd and in the host system. Usually the initrd is where provisioning is expected to happen as the root file system may itself be a dm-verity volume signed with one of the enrolled keys.

refsect1.title: Options

listitem.para: Show which certificates would be enrolled into which keyring, and the current state of the keyrings, without changing anything.

refsect1.para: If one or more KEYRING names are passed, only those keyrings are processed.

refsect1.title: Exit status
refsect1.para: On success, 0 is returned. This includes the cases where a keyring does not exist or was provisioned by an earlier boot stage already. 65 (EX_DATAERR) is returned if a certificate could not be used, for example because it is not signed by a key enrolled in an already sealed keyring. Enrollment failures never prevent the keyring from being sealed.

listitem.para: Kernel parameters leaving the respective keyring open for provisioning at boot. Without them the kernel seals the keyring empty and nothing can be enrolled.

refsect1.title: Security Considerations
refsect1.para: The trust the kernel puts into the enrolled certificates is only as strong as the trust in the files they were read from. Provisioning from the initrd of a signed Unified Kernel Image is the intended deployment.

Until the keyring is sealed, any privileged process may add any key to it. Once sealed, a privileged process may still remove keys from it, and add certificates signed by a key already enrolled. A soft reboot does not reset the keyrings. Note, if dm-verity is loaded as a module. When the module is loaded and unloaded the keyring will be destroyed and a new empty keyring will be created. The service runs about this. For high-security use-cases dm-verity should be built into the kernel.
